# Validation and freeze: why it keeps breaking, and the ordered fix

Status: proposal, 2026-10-04, after three complete inventories of the start/continue path (validation gates, capability-family vocabularies, hashed-type compatibility). Written after three consecutive user-visible outages in two days, all from the freeze/validate chain.

## 1. Observed failure chain

One feature task (native ComfyUI tools) produced four separate hard failures in sequence, each blocking the same user action:

1. `stored settings document is invalid: unknown field bridgeServerId` -> every command fails -> "Chat projection unavailable".
2. `workflow 'workflow.custom.3' is not executable: ... toolIds must reference tool.<name> or mcp:<server> bindings`.
3. `stored frozen Chat tool bindings failed integrity validation`.
4. Silent: the freeze path dropped both ComfyUI authoring helpers because a prefix test preceded the exact-id test.

Each was a different hand-written registry that had not been told about the new capability family. None was a tampering event; all four rejected artifacts this build itself wrote.

## 2. The design already forbids this

`aworkit.trusted_core.snapshot_freezer`, continuation clarification of 2026-09-19, states it directly: do not re-freeze tool metadata and then reject the Chat because installed metadata differs; do not pin tool schema, description, provider name or limits to the Chat; each invocation records the interface it actually used as evidence, without enforcing it later; explicit adapter compatibility is checked when dispatching a tool, never as an app-upgrade Chat-lockout gate. The container repeats it: missing capabilities never stop workflow preparation or execution.

The failure policy adds the second half: dispatch must degrade, because a rejected dispatch is a dead run.

The frozen record was designed as evidence. The implementation turned it into an enforcement gate that re-derives the past and rejects it. That, not the existence of freeze, is the defect class.

## 3. Measured surface

| Layer | Measured |
|---|---|
| Full closed-catalog validations of the selected document per message | 3 per start (`service.rs:1962` freeze, `pipeline.rs:3489` worker request validation, `pipeline.rs:2433` dispatch compile); 2 per follow-up. The 128 KiB bound is recomputed 3x per start. |
| Rules inside one such validation | 71 distinct error sites across ~15 helpers (`documents.rs:1436-2345`) |
| Frozen-record re-validations per command | ~2N-3N on a profile with N past Chats: `pending_effect_command_at_head` decodes and validates every stored frozen context and staged command on every command (`history.rs:686,699`); three further readers decode all again (`:629,:649,:1449`) |
| Tool settings frozen per action, in different representations | 2-3x: service-layer `FrozenToolBindingV1` (`workflow_tools.rs:10`, `current_configuration.rs:95`) and worker-layer `StoredFileToolBindingV1` (`tool_loop.rs:1204`, twice per fresh start) |
| Refusal sites in the four modules on the path | 184 (`documents.rs` 126, `history.rs` 51, `current_configuration.rs` 4, `workflow_tools.rs` 3) |
| Distinct user-visible refusal messages on the path | ~46 groups |
| Schema encoded twice, hand-maintained | ~17 `validate_*` fns / ~1000 lines Rust vs the 813-line `workflowExecution.ts`, ~45 equivalent rules |
| Capability-family vocabulary sites | 34 Rust + 13 TypeScript, 5 Rust<->TS drift pairs (one already drifted) |
| QA jobs covering "a profile from the previous build still opens its Chats" | none |

## 4. Verified traps where the build refuses its own output

1. **Save what you cannot run.** `save_workflow` gates on `validate_editable_workflow_graph` and applies the size bound only when the catalog also passes (`documents.rs:346,357`), while the editor deliberately preserves unknown node types (`WorkflowPropertiesPane.tsx:236`). A user can save a document this build refuses to start, against 71 rules it never showed them.
2. **One mid-Chat edit kills a running Chat.** For a follow-up the live library entry wins over the frozen snapshot; the snapshot is used only when the entry is gone (`current_configuration.rs:36-68`). Editing the saved workflow into a non-executable state blocks every later message.
3. **Send is gated by the default workflow, not the selection.** `service.rs:576-580` validates the library default, `:555` stores the failure as `disabled_reason`, and the composer disables Send (`composer.ts:44`).
4. **One bad old record poisons the rest.** `frozen_context` returns the first record matching the chat id, so an unreadable earlier record fails the read; `execution_for_chat_or_run` (`pipeline.rs:2776`) returns on the first matching prepared record; `deserialize_stored_file_tool_limit` migrates only one historical shape (`tool_loop.rs:686-720`).
5. **The write validates its own output.** `freeze_context` builds a record and immediately validates it (`history.rs:801-806`); `service.rs:1280` then compares the persisted record to the one it just passed, which is structurally dead code.
6. **A panic on the start path.** `service.rs:1995` `.expect("at least one model tier is resolved")`.

The counter-example sits in the same codebase: per-tool-call argument validation already degrades into a model-visible tool error, with the comment "Frozen argument validation is the recoverable execution boundary" (`tool_loop.rs:3449-3451`).

## 5. Compatibility: two hash rules inside one record

### Rule A (safe) versus Rule B (a migration cliff)

`canonical_hash` is RFC 8785 over the current `Serialize` impl. Reads (`decode_stored_frozen_context_record`, `history.rs:1866-1877`) use two different standards:

- **Rule A - stored bytes.** `record.context_hash` is compared with the JCS of the *raw stored JSON*. No schema change can move it.
- **Rule B - decoded struct.** Everything nested is recomputed from today's structs and compared with a stored hash: `workflow_snapshot_hash`, `model_tier_hash`, `provider_hash`, `model_hash` (`history.rs:1956-1959`), `tool_hash` per tool (`:2059`), and `project_configuration_hash` / `workspace_identity_hash` (`project_scope.rs:124-125`).

So adding `#[serde(default)]` (without a `skip_serializing_if` predicate) to `ProviderConfigurationV2` or `ModelConfigurationV2` makes `canonical_hash(&context.provider_snapshot) != context.provider_hash` for **every existing Chat**, while `context_hash` still passes. The record is rejected by a check that does not cover the bytes it hashes.

Accidental protections worth naming, because they must not be relied on: `workflow_snapshot` is a `Value`, so Rule B collapses to Rule A for it; and the types inside `definition`, `mcp_manifests` and `mcp_configurations` sit outside `tool_snapshot`, so only Rule A covers them.

### Blast radius

`frozen_context()` and `pending_effect_command_at_head()` decode **every** record in the profile-level aggregate with `?`. One unresumable legacy record therefore breaks context lookup for every Chat - and `freeze_context` re-reads all contexts at `:807`, so **starting a new Chat fails too**, and `ensure_history_summaries` (`:877-887`) can fail **at application open**. This is the mechanism behind the first symptom, "Chat projection unavailable".

### Ranked time bombs

1. `ProviderConfigurationV2` / `ModelConfigurationV2` - any additive default field invalidates `provider_hash` / `model_hash` for every Chat and also breaks the profile-wide scan.
2. `ToolOptions::is_default` - a field whose serde default differs from the derived `Default` makes `options` newly emitted for old frozen tools, so `tool_hash` mismatches.
3. `ProjectConfigurationV2` / `WorkspaceConfigurationV2` - the same structs have a Settings migration path but their frozen copies do not, so a Settings-side change silently bricks every project-scoped Chat.
4. `ModelTierConfigurationV2` / `ModelTierResolutionV2` - adding a field to an existing variant or to `ModelTargetV2` breaks `model_tier_hash`; adding a whole variant is safe.
5. `UiCommandInput` - `command_fingerprint` (`service.rs:4613`) digests in **field-declaration order**, so reordering fields breaks every started-but-uncommitted draft.

### Four digest rules share the `sha256:` prefix

`history`/`pipeline`/`tool_loop` `canonical_hash` are three duplicate copies of the JCS rule; `command_fingerprint` is declaration-order sensitive; `approvals::digest` relies on `serde_json`'s map being key-sorted, which holds today only because `preserve_order` is not enabled on a normal dependency edge - enabling it would silently invalidate every stored approval grant hash. `is_sha256` checks only length and hex, so no hash is ever verified cryptographically; and JCS coerces integers through f64, so two distinct values above 2^53 hash identically.

## 6. What is worth keeping

The freeze itself: one Chat, one pinned Run identity, provider/model binding, workspace, authority ceiling and committed evidence. The hashes as tamper and corruption evidence, once verified over bytes. Capability-host admission and manifest version/hash checks at dispatch. Approvals and authority. Credential reference metadata. The graph's semantic rules - a graph that cannot run should be refused once, with an explanation. Content-addressable snapshots and per-invocation evidence of the interface actually used.

What to delete is the re-validation of our own immutable artifacts: it adds nothing over a byte-exact hash check, multiplies the failure surface, and couples every schema change to a data-migration cliff.

## 7. Target design

1. **One trust boundary, validate once.** The core validates on save and at freeze; the verdict is committed with the document. The editor becomes a client of structured verdicts (path, rule, value) instead of a second implementation of the schema.
2. **Verify bytes afterwards.** Every read verifies the stored bytes; nothing re-derives a snapshot to compare it against a pinned expectation.
3. **One capability registry.** Each family provides `matches`, `descriptor`, `frozen_configuration`, `validate_frozen_shape` and `dispatch`; catalog, freeze, stored-record validation, admission and dispatch ask the registry. Adding a family is one implementation plus its tests.
4. **One digest rule.** A single hash function for durable artifacts, with the declaration-order-sensitive fingerprint removed.
5. **Versioned durable artifacts.** Version selects validation and migration; unknown newer versions become read-only with a notice. Unknown keys in durable records are dropped with a notice.
6. **Degrade and report on the run path**, per the policy that already exists.
7. **Read only what the command needs.** Index frozen records by chat id rather than decoding and validating every record in the profile.
8. **Diagnostics that name the thing:** field path, rule, offending value.

## 8. Ordered plan

**P0 - remove the outage class (hours, low risk).**
Verify nested snapshot hashes from stored bytes (Rule B -> Rule A); drop `deny_unknown_fields` on durable record types and drop unknown keys with a notice; scope frozen-record reads to the chat being used so one bad record cannot break the profile; add the compatibility QA job. Removes the app-wide lockout class and the "cannot open Aworkit at all" case.

**P1 - make validation incapable of killing a message (days, medium risk).**
Apply the failure policy to the freeze/validate chain, as per-tool-call argument validation already does; keep the single refusal at editor and freeze time where a human can act on it. Fix the traps in section 4: fall back to the frozen snapshot when the live entry is non-executable, stop gating Send on the default workflow, remove the start-path panic, stop validating what was just written. Removes "a validation error ate my message".

**P2 - one schema, one registry, one hash (weeks, staged).**
Capability registry and the family lists go; the editor consumes core verdicts and the TypeScript twin validator goes; one digest rule replaces the four; record version gate and migration; delete the redundant per-pass re-validations and cache the compiled pass by snapshot hash. Removes "adding a feature breaks existing Chats", most of the 184 refusal sites, and the O(N) cost per message.

## 9. Decision needed

Option A: P0 + P1, leaving the duplicated schema. It ends the pain the user experiences; it does not end the drift that produced it.
Option B: P0 -> P1 -> P2. It removes the class, at the cost of a staged refactor touching the editor validator, the catalog, freeze, admission and the stored-record validator.

Recommendation: P0 immediately, P1 next, P2 as its own task with the registry first.
